newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Fed seen raising US rates 2d half of 1997. [CORRECTED 20:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Fed seen raising US rates 2d half of 1997. [CORRECTED 20:43 GMT]

text.p: Recent signs of stronger U.S. economic growth and mounting inflationary pressures will prompt the Federal Reserve to raise rates by the cusp of second-half 1997, said most economists in a Reuters poll.
Most also predicted the bellwether Treasury bond's yield would creep higher amid anticipation of a Fed funds rate hike.

On average, 32 experts surveyed on Tuesday forecast the 30-year Treasury bond yield would fall (corrects from rise) to 6.76 percent by February 5, peak at about 6.84 percent in July, then slip back to 6.73 percent by January 1998.

In addition, the economists projected on average that the federal funds target rate would bump up from its current 5.25 percent rate to 5.50 percent by July and hold steady for the remainder of the year.
Over the past month or so, talk of a near-term rate hike had been subdued by signs that the economy grew at a moderate pace with few signs of inflationary wage pressures.
Now, many analysts said the whispers of a Fed tightening have risen to more audible levels.
"We had been expecting a cut in the fed funds rate mid-year (1997) this year up until the latest forecast," said Kurt Karl, chief economist of WEFA Group's U.S. forecasting center.
"As far as raising rates goes, I think there is more risk (the Fed) will raise rates this year at this point," said Karl, who is calling for steady monetary policy in 1997.
Unlike the December 17 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, which was deemed a "no-brainer" by analysts, the February encounter should produce more debate, economists said.
"It won't be like the December meeting, where you could take the day off for vacation and not worry about them doing anything," said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co.
So the question arises: Will the Fed raise rates in February?
For now, most experts are forecasting no move.
"We're seeing a little more supportive evidence for tightening ... (but) I don't think it has tipped the balance yet," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisers.
Looking at key data, Chan said he is projecting non-farm payrolls rose 150,000 and average hourly earnings advanced 0.3 percent in December.
"If my forecast is right, I think (the Fed) will be able to hold on and not raise rates at the February meeting," he said. "But I don't think they can hold off at the next one after that," he added.
Employment data is slated for release on Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.

David Blitzer, vice president and chief economist at Standard & Poor's Corp, said he is calling for the central bank to tighten in two quarter-point steps in 1997 -- one in March and one in the second quarter.
"That will slightly slow the economy in the second half of the year," he said.

Blitzer noted there is very little room for strong growth because we are running at capacity or very close to it. He did say, however, consumer spending, the largest component of gross domestic product, should continue to show reasonable strength.
"We have very few idle resources and trying to grow even at 3.0 percent for a couple of quarters is enough to make the Fed nervous." he said.
Feb5 Apr Jul Jan Feb5 Apr Jul Jan
*fed funds averages rounded to nearest quarter-point
